$comment: R1733 — the analysis tool's DASHBOARD BOARD and the gesture that populates
it, written down once, in neutral vocabulary, as the behaviour reference
draws it.
WHY THIS IS A FILE AND NOT A RUST CONSTANT. The reason the four spec files
beside it are. The screen's own `spec` module is what a RUNNING screen
needs — paint tags, catalogue rows, the wording of a refusal. A
specification written there would be written by the same hand in the same
edit as the thing under test, so a conformance check would be asking the
subject for the answer.
EXTRACTION. The reference is not in this repository and must not be. The
procedure is the recorded one: the document is a single JSON string line
holding the whole application as one inline script plus its markup.
Measured 2026-08-20 by extracting both and reading the palette drawer, the
canvas element's drag handlers and the two blocks the canvas draws while a
placement is in flight.
WHAT THIS ROUND IS ABOUT. The reference's palette row is `draggable` and
its canvas takes the drop; this build could only ever ADD from a palette
row, which was the last first-pass reproduction gap its GUI element census
had open. Measured in the reference: the palette row carries BOTH — a drag
start and a click that adds — so reproducing the drag is an addition and
not a replacement. That distinction is load-bearing here, because the
reference has zero keyboard bindings and moving its pointer-only gesture
over INSTEAD of the action would take the palette away from a reader who
cannot drag.
VOCABULARY. The reference's product and protocol words are replaced by the
words the tool class uses generally. Structure and behaviour are what is
being reproduced; the wording is not. The titles below are this file's
words for what is drawn — the reference labels almost none of these parts —
and the file says so rather than pretending otherwise.
THE TWO HALVES. Each surface carries `canon` — what the reference has — and
`owed` — where this build differs, each entry carrying the round that
accepted it and why. The gate asserts the difference between the built
surface and `canon` is EXACTLY `owed`, so a new divergence fails and so
does an owed one that has been paid off without this file being told.
OWED RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. A part this build has and the reference does
not is a divergence too, and is recorded here rather than deleted: the
standing order rule is that the reference is what must be REPRODUCED and
is not a ceiling, so something present here and absent there stays and says
why.
One row of the widget palette — the SOURCE half of the gesture. The
reference draws the row as a single draggable element carrying four
things, and the row is also the click target that adds without a drag.
Read back from the paint in reading order: these four sit beside each
other on one line, which is what reading order is the rule for.

$comment: What the board puts on screen while a palette footprint is being carried
over it. These parts are LAYERS, not a row, so the order specified is the
z-order and the build's side is read in paint order — see the framework's
`painted_stack`, which exists because reading order over four overlapping
rectangles is arithmetic on coordinates that mean nothing.
Measured in the reference: while a placement is in flight it raises a
per-cell dashed overlay, pushes a snap rectangle into the grid at the
cell a release would use, and covers the whole canvas with a dashed frame
that says in words what letting go does. It also grows the overlay by
THREE rows rather than one, so there is somewhere to drop below what is
already placed; that is behaviour rather than a part, and the screen's
own gate asserts it.

canon.title: the cell grid, raised while a placement is in flight
the mark at the cell a release would use
the whole-canvas invitation saying a release places it

owed.sentence: part 3 `chip` is on the surface and no specification declares it
owed.why: A second-pass improvement, kept deliberately. The reference is a browser prototype, so while a palette row is carried the browser draws its own drag image and the application draws nothing that names what is in hand. A framework that paints its own scene has no such gift: without this chip the only thing on screen is a mark at a cell, and a person who has picked up the wrong row learns it on release. R1726 built the chip for the other drag and named the same reason; the standing order rule keeps what the reference lacks.

$comment: The snap mark itself. The reference draws a dashed accent rectangle
spanning the carried footprint, centred on a six-dot grip glyph and the
destination cell in parentheses — the same glyph its rows are dragged by,
so the mark and the handle read as the same gesture.
Two parts side by side, so this one IS a reading-order surface.

canon.title: the grip glyph, the same one a row is dragged by

$comment: R1734 — WHAT THE BOARD ACCEPTS, declared as data and answerable before
anything is picked up.
The three surfaces above pin what the gesture DRAWS. This one pins what
the board SAYS about the gesture, which is the half no prototype has:
the reference declares acceptance by attaching handlers, so the only way
to learn what its board takes is to drag something onto it and watch. A
mature retained-mode toolkit is no better here — probed offscreen at
6.11.1, a widget's acceptance is one boolean, per-part acceptance is a
second boolean that names no kind at all, and the members that do name
kinds are absent from the runtime metaobject a generic reader walks.
So this surface is a SECOND-PASS addition by the standing order rule:
the reference has nothing here to reproduce, and we keep it. It is
pinned anyway, because a capability with no specification is a
capability the next round can quietly drop.
Read back from the DECLARATION the running screen publishes at `$drop`,
not from a constant in the test — the point of the pin is that the
screen's answer is the reviewed one.
One clause. Both of its actions are real: a palette row is COPIED (the
row stays and the board gains a card) and a card already placed is
MOVED. The region is the whole surface because this screen hit-tests
itself and paints one scene tag, so a drop point over it carries no
sub-part for a part clause to match — declaring parts the wire cannot
resolve would publish a promise the router could not keep.

canon.title: copy or move, anywhere on the surface
